name: Forgiving platformer jump (Celeste-style)
keywords: platformer jump coyote time jump buffer variable jump height game feel tight controls responsive celeste mario hollow knight
feel: Jumping feels responsive and fair: the game does what you meant, not exactly what you pressed. Players blame themselves, not the controls.
seen_in: Celeste, Super Meat Boy, Hollow Knight, most modern platformers.
how:
Four small rules, all visible in Celeste's Player.cs (MIT, released by its developer as a learning resource):
- Coyote time: you can still jump for 0.1 s after walking off a ledge (JumpGraceTime = 0.1).
- Jump buffering: a jump pressed slightly before landing still happens (Celeste's input buffer is about 0.08 s).
- Variable height: while the button is held the jump keeps its upward speed for up to 0.2 s (VarJumpTime); letting go cuts it short.
- Floaty apex: near the top of a held jump (vertical speed under 40 px/s in Celeste) gravity is halved, giving a moment of hang time to aim.
Running approaches top speed with acceleration rather than snapping to it, and air control is reduced (AirMult = 0.65).
knobs: Coyote/buffer windows (0.05-0.15 s: bigger = more forgiving). Gravity vs jump speed (higher both = snappier). Air multiplier (lower = more committed jumps). Apex threshold (bigger = floatier).

name: Invincibility frames (i-frames) after getting hit
keywords: iframes invincibility invulnerable damage hit blink flash health knockback mercy hurt
feel: Getting hit is a setback, not a death spiral: you get a moment to recover, and the blinking tells you you're safe for now.
seen_in: Mega Man, Castlevania, Hollow Knight, Zelda, almost every action game with health.
how: After taking damage, ignore further damage for a short window (often 0.5-1.5 s) and make the character blink so the player can see it. Many games also knock the player back away from the hit so they aren't stuck inside the enemy.
knobs: Window length (longer = more forgiving). Blink rate. Knockback strength. Whether i-frames also apply to hazards like spikes.
source: Common practice; described here from the design.

name: Stamina that gates actions (Souls-style)
keywords: stamina endurance fatigue souls dark souls elden ring bloodborne commitment attack dodge roll resource management combat
feel: Every attack and dodge is a decision. You can't mash: overcommitting leaves you exhausted and open, so fights become a rhythm of attack, retreat and recover.
seen_in: Dark Souls, Elden Ring, Sekiro (as posture), Monster Hunter; Morrowind's fatigue is an ancestor.
how: Actions cost stamina. In the Souls games an action is allowed while stamina is above zero even if it costs more than you have (so the last swing is always possible, but leaves you empty). Stamina regenerates only after a short delay since the last spend, which is what punishes button mashing. Blocking slows regeneration.
knobs: Regen delay (longer = more punishing). Regen rate. Whether an action needs the full cost or just any stamina. Costs per action (heavier weapon = more cost).
source: Design described from the games; Morrowind's fatigue system in OpenMW (GPL-3.0) for comparison.

name: Readable, fair enemy AI (Doom-style)
keywords: enemy ai monster chase attack fair readable telegraph reaction time doom shooter behavior state
feel: Enemies feel dangerous but fair: they react a beat after seeing you, don't spam attacks, and move in committed bursts you can read and dodge.
seen_in: Doom (1993) and countless action games since.
how:
From Doom's A_Chase in p_enemy.c (GPL-2.0, released by id Software):
- reactiontime: a monster won't attack until a short delay after it notices you, giving you time to respond.
- MF_JUSTATTACKED: after attacking, the next think is spent moving, never attacking twice in a row.
- movecount: a monster commits to a direction for several steps before picking a new one, so movement is readable rather than jittery.
- P_CheckMissileRange: the chance to shoot falls with distance (and skips the check entirely when too far), so close range is more dangerous than far.
knobs: Reaction time. Minimum time between attacks. How long it commits to a direction. Attack chance vs distance. Speed.

name: Skills that grow by using them (Bethesda-style)
keywords: skill leveling learn by doing use based progression elder scrolls skyrim morrowind oblivion rpg character growth experience
feel: You become what you do: sneak a lot and you get sneaky. Progress feels earned and personal, and players shape their character through play instead of menus.
seen_in: The Elder Scrolls (Morrowind, Oblivion, Skyrim), RuneScape, Final Fantasy II.
how:
From OpenMW's NpcStats (GPL-3.0), the open reimplementation of Morrowind:
- Each use of a skill adds progress (different actions give different amounts).
- A skill levels up when progress reaches (1 + current level) x a class factor, so higher skills take longer: major skills use a factor below 1 (faster), miscellaneous skills above 1 (slower).
- Raising your important skills enough times raises your overall character level.
knobs: Progress per use. The growth curve (linear here; steeper curves slow late game). Which skills count as 'major'. Caps.

name: Camera that looks ahead
keywords: camera follow lookahead smooth platformer view framing deadzone camera2d
feel: You can see where you're going, not where you've been. The camera feels calm instead of glued to the player.
seen_in: Super Mario World, SuperTux, Sonic, most side-scrollers.
how: SuperTux's camera.cpp (GPL-3.0) shifts the view toward the direction the player is moving (lookahead) and eases into it rather than snapping. Godot's Camera2D already does smoothing and drag margins (a dead zone the player can move inside without the camera moving); a lookahead offset on top makes the view lead the player.
knobs: Lookahead distance. How quickly the offset eases. Position smoothing speed. Drag margins (dead zone size).

name: Escalating enemy waves
keywords: waves spawner tower defense survival horde difficulty ramp escalation vampire survivors mindustry
feel: Tension builds steadily: each wave is a little harder than the last, with breathers in between to plan and recover.
seen_in: Mindustry, Plants vs. Zombies, Vampire Survivors, tower defense games, horde modes.
how: Mindustry (GPL-3.0) defines waves as groups of enemies that start at some wave, grow by a fixed amount per wave, and stop growing at a cap; a countdown between waves gives players time to build. The core loop: count grows each wave, the break between waves gives a rhythm of tension and release.
knobs: Starting count. Growth per wave. Cap. Time between waves. Spawn spread within a wave.

name: Weighted loot tables
keywords: loot drop random rarity weighted chance items treasure diablo roguelike reward
feel: Rewards feel exciting because rare things are rare: most drops are ordinary, so the occasional rare one is a thrill.
seen_in: Diablo, Borderlands, Shattered Pixel Dungeon, every loot game.
how: Give each possible drop a weight; pick a random number up to the total weight and walk the list. Shattered Pixel Dungeon's Generator (GPL-3.0) goes further: after an item category drops, its weight is reduced so you don't get five of the same kind in a row, and it recovers over time (a 'deck' feel that avoids streaks).
knobs: Weights per rarity. Whether drops 'remember' recent results (streak protection). Pity timers (a guaranteed rare after N misses).

name: Hit stop and screen shake (game juice)
keywords: juice game feel hit stop freeze frame screen shake impact feedback punchy combat polish
feel: Hits feel heavy and impactful. A tiny freeze on impact plus a short shake makes the player FEEL the blow, even with simple art.
seen_in: Celeste, Hollow Knight, Street Fighter, Vlambeer games (Nuclear Throne), Hades.
how: Hit stop: on a strong hit, slow time almost to zero for a few hundredths of a second (Celeste freezes the whole game for ~0.05 s on dashes and hits). Screen shake: offset the camera by a random amount that decays quickly. Both must be SHORT; too much feels sluggish or nauseating. Use real time for the freeze, since game time is what you're slowing.
knobs: Freeze length (0.03-0.1 s). Shake strength and decay. Only on important hits, or it stops meaning anything.
source: Common practice; Celeste's freeze frames in Player.cs (MIT).

name: Rest points / bonfires
keywords: checkpoint bonfire save point rest respawn souls dark souls elden ring grace hollow knight bench
feel: Relief and dread at once: reaching one feels like safety and progress, but resting brings enemies back, so every trip out is a risk you choose.
seen_in: Dark Souls (bonfires), Elden Ring (sites of grace), Hollow Knight (benches), Resident Evil (typewriters).
how: A rest point sets where you respawn, restores health and healing items, and (in Souls games) resets the world's enemies. The spacing between them is the real difficulty dial: the run from the last bonfire to the boss IS part of the challenge. Shortcuts that loop back to a rest point are the reward for exploring.
knobs: Distance between rest points. What resting restores. Whether resting respawns enemies. Whether dying costs something (Souls drops your currency where you died, so you can win it back).

name: Saving and loading progress
keywords: save load progress persist high score settings config file continue
feel: Players trust the game with their time. Losing progress is one of the fastest ways to lose a player.
seen_in: Every game longer than a few minutes.
how: Godot's ConfigFile reads and writes simple sections of key=value pairs to user://, which is the player's own save folder on any platform. Save at natural moments (rest points, level ends) and also when quitting.
knobs: When to save (autosave vs manual). How many slots. What to store (only what you can't recompute).

name: Turns by time spent (speed-based turn order)
keywords: turn based roguelike turn order initiative speed time scheduler tactics actors energy
feel: Speed matters in a turn-based game: a fast rat gets two moves for your one, a slowed enemy falls behind, and players can reason about it.
seen_in: Shattered Pixel Dungeon, NetHack, Final Fantasy's ATB, many tactics games.
how: In Shattered Pixel Dungeon's Actor.java (GPL-3.0), every actor has a 'time'. Acting spends time (a normal move costs 1 TICK; a slow actor spends more, a hasted one less). The scheduler always lets the actor with the LOWEST time act next. There is no global 'round': speed differences fall out naturally.
knobs: Base action cost. Speed modifiers. Tie-breaking (SPD gives the player priority on equal time).

name: Interconnected world with shortcuts (Souls-style level design)
keywords: level design shortcuts interconnected world metroidvania dark souls hollow knight one way door unlock loop exploration
feel: 'Oh, it's THAT door!' Opening a shortcut back to somewhere familiar is a burst of relief and understanding: the world clicks together in your head.
seen_in: Dark Souls (Firelink Shrine, the Undead Parish elevator), Hollow Knight, Super Metroid, Resident Evil's mansion.
how: Areas loop back on themselves. Shortcuts are usually one-way: locked from the safe side, opened from the dangerous side after you've pushed through (a door that only opens from one side, a ladder you kick down, an elevator). This rewards pushing forward and shortens the run back to the rest point, so difficulty drops as mastery of the space grows. Landmarks visible from far away let players plan routes.
knobs: How far you push before a shortcut appears. How many loops lead back to the same hub. Whether the map is shown or left to memory.

name: Emergent simulation and radiant worlds (Bethesda-style)
keywords: open world sandbox emergent simulation radiant ai npc schedules physics skyrim fallout oblivion immersive sim systems
feel: The world feels alive and goes on without you: NPCs have routines, systems collide in unscripted ways, and players tell their own stories ('a giant launched me into the sky').
seen_in: Skyrim, Oblivion (Radiant AI), Fallout, Breath of the Wild (chemistry engine), immersive sims like Deus Ex and Prey.
how: Instead of scripting every event, give objects and characters simple rules (NPCs follow daily schedules, fire spreads to grass, items have physics) and let them interact. Quests can be generated from templates ('clear a random cave', 'deliver to a random NPC'). The design work is in choosing rules that combine interestingly and giving players tools that touch many systems. The trade-off: less control over pacing and more bugs, which players often forgive (or love) when the freedom is real.
knobs: How many systems interact. How much is scripted vs emergent. How much the world reacts to the player's reputation and choices.

name: Easy to learn, hard to master
keywords: depth simple rules mastery skill ceiling tetris chess elegant design accessible competitive
feel: Anyone can start playing in seconds, but experts keep finding new depth for years.
seen_in: Tetris, Pac-Man, Rocket League, Super Smash Bros., chess.
how: A tiny set of rules, explained by playing, with consequences that combine deeply. In Tetris, the rules fit in a sentence, but speed, stacking strategy and T-spins create an enormous skill range. Design moves: few inputs, consistent physics or rules with no exceptions, and a difficulty that ramps (Tetris gets faster) so the game meets every player at their level.
knobs: Number of verbs/inputs. How fast difficulty ramps. Whether advanced techniques are taught or discovered.

name: Death as progress (roguelite loop)
keywords: roguelike roguelite permadeath run based meta progression hades dead cells binding of isaac slay the spire replayability
feel: Dying stings but never wastes your time: every run teaches you something or unlocks something, so 'one more run' is irresistible.
seen_in: Hades, Dead Cells, Slay the Spire, The Binding of Isaac, Rogue Legacy.
how: Short runs with randomized layouts and rewards, so every attempt is different. Permanent unlocks or story progress carried between runs (Hades advances its story when you die). Builds come from combining random upgrades, so players learn synergies. Hades' key insight: making death a narrative event turns failure into content.
knobs: Run length. How much carries over (none = roguelike, some = roguelite). How random vs. chosen the upgrades are.

name: Cozy games: low pressure, high comfort
keywords: cozy wholesome relaxing farming life sim stardew animal crossing no fail calm daily routine
feel: Safe, warm and unhurried. Players come back to relax, not to be challenged; small daily goals and gentle progress feel rewarding.
seen_in: Stardew Valley, Animal Crossing, A Short Hike, Unpacking.
how: No harsh failure states (at worst you lose a day or some time). Clear, small goals with a daily rhythm. Collections and customization that reflect the player. Characters who remember you. Soft colors, gentle sounds, and the freedom to ignore any goal. Stardew grew from its developer's love of Harvest Moon, rebuilt to fix what frustrated him.
knobs: How much time pressure (energy, seasons). How many systems to juggle. How much the world responds to the player.

name: Teaching without tutorials (level 1-1 design)
keywords: tutorial onboarding teach player level design first level mario 1-1 show dont tell learning curve
feel: Players feel clever: they figure things out themselves instead of reading instructions.
seen_in: Super Mario Bros. World 1-1, Portal's test chambers, Celeste's early screens, Hollow Knight.
how: Introduce one idea at a time in a safe space, then test it with a small twist, then combine it with something learned earlier. In World 1-1 the first Goomba walks toward you on open ground where jumping is the obvious answer; the first mushroom bounces into a pipe so you can't miss it. Portal introduces each mechanic alone in a chamber before mixing them.
knobs: How safe the first encounter is. How quickly ideas get combined. Whether there's any text at all.

sections.Intro:
Dark Souls is a 2011 action role-playing game developed by FromSoftware and published by Namco Bandai Games. It is the first game in the Dark Souls series and a spiritual successor to FromSoftware's Demon's Souls. Set in the kingdom of Lordran, the game follows the Chosen Undead, who escapes from the Northern Undead Asylum and travels through Lordran to discover the fate of the undead. Gameplay centres on exploration, deliberate combat, character customisation, and online interactions including messages, cooperative play, and invasions.
After its original release for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360, a Windows port featuring additional content, titled the Prepare to Die Edition, was released in August 2012. That additional content was released separately for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 versions as the downloadable content pack Artorias of the Abyss in October 2012. A remastered version was released for PlayStation 4, Windows, Xbox One, and Nintendo Switch in 2018.
Dark Souls has been cited as one of the greatest video games ever made. Critics praised the depth of its combat, intricate level design, and use of flavour text, while responses to its high level of difficulty were divided. The original Windows version was less well received, with criticism directed at technical issues. By April 2013, the game had sold 2.37 million copies worldwide. Its success led to two sequels, Dark Souls II (2014) and Dark Souls III (2016).
sections.Gameplay:
Dark Souls is a third-person action role-playing game. The player explores Lordran, a single interconnected world divided into distinct regions and linked by unlockable shortcuts. Areas can often be approached through multiple routes, although some paths are locked until the player meets certain prerequisites. The game encourages cautious exploration, as progress often depends on learning enemy placement, attack patterns, and alternative routes through repeated attempts.
Bonfires serve as checkpoints and sites for character management. Resting at a bonfire restores the player character's health and Estus Flask charges, and allows the player to level up, attune magic, and repair or upgrade equipment. Resting also respawns most enemies, excluding bosses, mini-bosses, and killed non-player characters.
Combat involves melee and ranged weapons, defensive manoeuvres, and magic. The player can block, dodge roll, backstep, parry, or attack with weapons such as swords, spears, bows, and crossbows. Magic is divided into sorceries, miracles, and pyromancies. Unlike many role-playing games, spells are not cast from a mana pool; each attuned spell instead has a limited number of uses, which are restored when the player rests at a bonfire. Equipment and combat abilities can be altered through levelling, weapon upgrades, armour, and equipment choices.
Defeating enemies grants souls, which function as both currency and experience points. When the player dies, the character returns to the last bonfire and drops any carried souls and humanity at the place of death. The player can recover them by reaching the resulting bloodstain, but loses them permanently after dying again before doing so.
sections.Gameplay / Multiplayer:
Dark Souls integrates online features into the single-player world. The player can see ghostly images of other players, activate bloodstains that show how other players died, and leave messages using preset phrases. Direct multiplayer includes cooperative summoning and player-versus-player invasions.
The humanity system controls access to some online features. Dying in human form returns the character to undead form. The player can restore human form at a bonfire by consuming humanity, allowing them to summon other players and certain non-player characters for assistance, but also exposing them to invasions. The game can still be completed in undead form.
Covenants, optional factions encountered during the game, can affect multiplayer goals, rewards, and interactions. Some covenants encourage cooperative play, while others focus on invasions or other forms of player-versus-player interaction.
In January 2022, online services for the Windows versions of the Dark Souls games were disabled after a security exploit was found. Online multiplayer for the original Windows Prepare to Die Edition was later permanently disabled, while online features for Dark Souls: Remastered on Windows were restored in November 2022.
sections.Synopsis / Setting:
Dark Souls is set in Lordran, a decaying kingdom near the end of the Age of Fire. In the opening cutscene, the world is first described as an unchanging Age of Ancients inhabited by Everlasting Dragons. The First Flame then appears, bringing disparity: heat and cold, life and death, and light and dark. Several beings find powerful souls within the flame, including Gwyn, Lord of Sunlight; the Witch of Izalith; Gravelord Nito, the first of the dead; and the Furtive Pygmy, who finds the Dark Soul. 
Gwyn, the Witch, Nito, and the scaleless dragon Seath overthrow the dragons, beginning the Age of Fire. As the First Flame fades, Gwyn sacrifices himself to preserve it. The game begins much later, when humans marked by the Darksign are cursed to resurrect after death and eventually lose their minds, becoming hollow.
sections.Synopsis / Setting / Plot:
The opening cutscene establishes the premise of the game. Everlasting Dragons once ruled over the world during the "Age of Ancients." A primordial fire known as the First Flame manifests in the world, establishing a distinction between life and death, and light and dark. A being known as Gwyn happens upon the First Flame and along with his allies use their new power to destroy the dragons and take control over the world, while the Furtive Pygmy is said to be forgotten, and thus begins the "Age of Fire." Over time, as the First Flame begins to fade while humans rise in power, Gwyn sacrifices himself to prolong the Age of Fire. The main story takes place towards the end of this second Age of Fire, at which point humanity is said to be afflicted with an undead curse related to a symbol on their bodies known as the Darksign. Those humans afflicted with the undead curse were perpetually resurrect after death until they eventually lose their minds, a process referred to as "hollowing."
The player character is a cursed undead, locked away in an undead asylum. After escaping the asylum, the player travels to Lordran to ring the Bells of Awakening. The bells awaken Kingseeker Frampt who tells the player to ascend to Anor Londo, the home of the Gods. After fighting through the nearly abandoned city, the player discovers the daughter of Gwyn, Gwynevere, who instructs the player to succeed Lord Gwyn and fulfill the prophecy. To accomplish this, the player must acquire the souls of Gwynn's primordial allies and return them to the flame in order to rekindle it. Optionally, the player may encounter Darkstalker Kaathe, who encourages the player not to link the fire but to let it die out and usher in the Age of Dark instead. After acquiring all the Lord Souls, the player travels to the Kiln of the First Flame to battle Gwyn, who had been reduced to a soulless husk. Once Gwyn has been defeated, the player has the choice of linking the flame to preserve the Age of Fire or letting it die out to instigate the Age of Dark.
sections.Synopsis / Setting / Plot / Artorias of: In the Artorias of the Abyss expansion, the player character is drawn into the past to the ruined land of Oolacile. There, they attempt to rescue Princess Dusk of Oolacile and investigate the fate of Knight Artorias, who had sought to confront the Abyss. The player character finds Artorias corrupted after being defeated by Manus, Father of the Abyss. After defeating Artorias and Manus, the player character rescues Dusk, while present-day legends continue to credit Artorias with stopping the Abyss.
sections.Development:
Dark Souls was developed by FromSoftware and directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki, who also served as one of its producers. The game followed FromSoftware's 2009 action role-playing game Demon's Souls. Before release, Miyazaki said that Dark Souls was not a sequel to Demon's Souls, but a new game with similar concepts made by the same director and producers. Namco Bandai producers Daisuke Uchiyama and Kei Hirono similarly described it as a spiritual successor rather than a direct sequel, while noting that it shared much of the same development team and gameplay concept. Namco Bandai Games handled international publishing, while FromSoftware published the game in Japan.
Miyazaki said that the team intended to retain and increase the challenge associated with Demon's Souls, but not simply by making the game harder. Instead, the goal was to give players freedom to experiment with strategies and feel rewarded for overcoming obstacles. He described bonfires, referred to before release as "Beacon Fires", as recovery and respawn points that also served as rare places of warmth in the game's dark fantasy world.
The game's art direction was developed through a mixture of broad prompts and direct oversight. Miyazaki said that, during the early concept stage, he gave artists simple "image words" and allowed them to produce designs freely, after which he selected, revised, or incorporated their ideas. When designs had a more specific gameplay or worldbuilding function, he gave more detailed instructions about their use and placement. Miyazaki said he worked directly with each designer rather than assigning a single intermediary to manage the visual direction.
Miyazaki described the game's visual design as organised around several broad themes: gods and knights centred on Anor Londo, chaos and demons centred on Lost Izalith, death and decay centred on Gravelord Nito, and the ancient dragons. He also said he sought "refinement and elegance" in the game's designs, even in grotesque or decayed areas. Some locations drew on real-world architecture; a designer cited Milan Cathedral as a reference for Anor Londo's buttresses, while Miyazaki said that New Londo Ruins was based partly on Mont-Saint-Michel in Normandy, France.
Miyazaki later said that the manga series Berserk had influenced Dark Souls, although he said gameplay remained his first priority during the design process.
sections.Reception / Original release:
Dark Souls received positive reviews from critics upon its release. One of the reviewers for Dark Souls described it as "a very hardcore dark-fantasy [role-playing game]" that is "role-playing right down to the roots", and stated that the "massive field map and powerful enemies serve to rev up both your sense of adventure and your sense of dread." Another reviewer said that "the sheer happiness you get after the trial-and-error pays off and you overcome the challenge is absolutely impossible to replicate."
GameSpot praised the online system and the sense of jubilation when conquering boss fights after numerous failed attempts. They also suggested that casual gamers may struggle to progress, whereas role-playing game enthusiasts will thrive on the difficulty. IGN complimented the level design, variety, strong emphasis on online features, excessively dark tone and atmosphere, and deep gameplay. While praising the extreme difficulty, they stated that "there's a difference between punishing, and downright unfair." Eurogamer also applauded the level design and atmosphere while noting that the game's difficulty might not appeal to casual gamers.
Edge retroactively awarded the game 10 out of 10 in their October 2013 20th anniversary issue, stating that the breadth and quality of the game's design had overruled complaints about its difficulty.
Game Informer Phil Kollar opined that "the frustration in Dark Souls arises from how [late '00s and early 2010s] games have conditioned us. Gamers are used to handholding tutorials that walk you through every aspect of a game’s mechanics." While complimenting the game's notoriously steep difficulty curve, Kollar was less favourable toward its "overall lack of direction".
In a review of Dark Souls in Black Gate, Connor Gormley said "I can't help but smile at all the things I've done in this game, from the serious and atmospheric, to the actually kind of stupid, like losing a fist fight with a giant mushroom man who I like to imagine has a thick cockney accent. I've given very few examples of the game's lore by design, because half of the fun is finding that out for yourself, at least if you're in it for the fantasy. It's an experience, one fueled by creativity and ingenuity, and it's one that I urge you to go out and at least try, regular gamer or not."
Namco Bandai's yearly financial report stated that the game sold 1.19 million units in the United States and Europe by March 2012. FromSoftware announced in April 2013 that the game had sold 2.37 million units worldwide.
Game writer Erik Wolpaw, an early proponent of the Souls series going back to 2009's Demon's Souls, said the game was his favourite of 2011.
sections.Reception / Original release / Later rel:
In GameSpy's review, the original Windows port was referred to as "shabby", citing the game's limit of 30 frames per second, poor mouse and keyboard controls, and nonadjustable resolution. However, the expanded content was praised, giving the game an overall favourable review. 
Eurogamer commented on the quality of the port, stating: "Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition does not come with the technical options you would expect from a well-engineered PC game, because it's a port of a console game, and that's all FromSoftware ever promised to deliver. Anyone who passes up Dark Souls for this reason is cutting off their nose to spite their neckbeard of a face." One of the producers of Dark Souls II, Takeshi Miyazoe, responded to the criticism of the PC version by saying:

This is going to sound bad but our main priority was to get the game onto the PC as fast as possible, because people wanted it on the PC. The PC market in Japan is so minimal that originally there were no plans to make it on the PC, but with the strong petition from the North American and European fans, even with the lack of experience of working on a PC platform we still did our best to try to get it out as fast as possible. [The problems] were expected to a certain extent.
We did know there were PC-specific features like key-mapping and use of the mouse and keyboard, high resolution and higher frame rate, stuff like that, but... It's not that we ignored it, but it would have taken too much time for us to implement it, test it and get it up to the level people expected. It was more of a publisher (Namco Bandai) decision to say, "Guys, don't worry about this – let's just get it out and see how this works on PC."
Dark Souls: Remastered received "generally favorable" reviews from critics, according to review aggregator Metacritic. Critics praised the improved visuals and performance, while criticism was directed towards the lack of an effective anti-cheat system and the PC version's price despite few significant changes. It sold 71,739 copies in Japan during the week of its release, making it the best-selling game in the country at the time.

Game Revolution gave Dark Souls the Community Choice Game of the Year award. IncGamers also gave it the "Game of the Year" award. Q-Games' Dylan Cuthbert and Double Fine Productions' Brad Muir chose Dark Souls as Game of the Year. Electronic Gaming Monthly's Eric L. Patterson chose it as Game of the Year. GameTrailers gave it the "Best Role-Playing Game" award while also nominating it for the "Best Multiplayer Game", "Best Trailer", and "Game of the Year" awards. GameZone gave the game the "Best Action/Adventure" award and chose it as the runner-up for the "Best RPG" award. At the 15th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards (now known as the D.I.C.E. Awards), the Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences nominated Dark Souls for "Role-Playing/Massively Multiplayer Game of the Year".
The Daily Telegraph gave the game the "Best Integration of Online Features" award and nominated it for the awards of "Best Director" (Hidetaka Miyazaki), "Best Level Design", "Best Sound Design", "Best Original Score" (Motoi Sakuraba), "Best Developer" (FromSoftware), and "Game of the Year". TeamXbox gave it an honourable mention as the runner-up for the "Best RPG" award. 1UP.com gave it the "Most Rewarding Game" award. Game Informer gave it the award for "Best Boss Fight" (Sif). It also received the "Best Boss Fights" awards from GameSpot, including the Editors' Choice and Readers' Choice awards. Famitsu gave it an Award of Excellence in its 2012 awards ceremony.
In 2013, Digital Spy named Dark Souls the best game of the seventh console generation. In 2014, Edge magazine named Dark Souls the best game of the seventh generation of game consoles, noting that while some may initially tire of it, "We've yet to meet a single player for whom persistence has not been enough to transform apathy into all-consuming love." In September 2015, Dark Souls topped the Edge's special issue The 100 Greatest Videogames. 
In 2015, the game placed first on GamesRadar+'s "The 100 best games ever" list. The game was also put first on USgamer's The 15 Best Games Since 2000 list. The game was titled the "Best RPG on PC" by Rock, Paper, Shotgun. In 2016, Dark Souls placed fifth on PC Gamer's "Best RPGs of all time" list. In 2021, the game was voted the Ultimate Game of All Time at the Golden Joystick Awards.

After its original release for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360, a Windows port featuring additional content, titled the Prepare to Die Edition, was released in August 2012. That additional content was released separately for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 versions as the downloadable content pack Artorias of the Abyss in October 2012. A remastered version was released for PlayStation 4, Windows, Xbox One, and Nintendo Switch in 2018.
Dark Souls has been cited as one of the greatest video games ever made. sections.Gameplay:
Dark Souls is a third-person action role-playing game. The player explores Lordran, a single interconnected world divided into distinct regions and linked by unlockable shortcuts. Areas can often be approached through multiple routes, although some paths are locked until the player meets certain prerequisites. Bonfires serve as checkpoints and sites for character management. Resting at a bonfire restores the player character's health and Estus Flask charges, and allows the player to level up, attune magic, and repair or upgrade equipment. Combat involves melee and ranged weapons, defensive manoeuvres, and magic. The player can block, dodge roll, backstep, parry, or attack with weapons such as swords, spears, bows, and crossbows. Covenants, optional factions encountered during the game, can affect multiplayer goals, rewards, and interactions. Some covenants encourage cooperative play, while others focus on invasions or other forms of player-versus-player interaction.

sections.Reception / Original release:
Dark Souls received positive reviews from critics upon its release. One of the reviewers for Dark Souls described it as "a very hardcore dark-fantasy [role-playing game]" that is "role-playing right down to the roots", and stated that the "massive field map and powerful enemies serve to rev up both your sense of adventure and your sense of dread." Another reviewer said that "the sheer happiness you get after the trial-and-error pays off and you overcome the challenge is absolutely impossible to replicate."
GameSpot praised the online system and the sense of jubilation when conquering boss fights after numerous failed attempts. They also suggested that casual gamers may struggle to progress, whereas role-playing game enthusiasts will thrive on the difficulty. IGN complimented the level design, variety, strong emphasis on online features, excessively dark tone and atmosphere, and deep gameplay. While praising the extreme difficulty, they stated that "there's a difference between punishing, and downright unfair." Eurogamer also applauded the level design and atmosphere while noting that the game's difficulty might not appeal to casual gamers.
Edge retroactively awarded the game 10 out of 10 in their October 2013 20th anniversary issue, stating that the breadth and quality of the game's design had overruled complaints about its difficulty.
Game Informer Phil Kollar opined that "the frustration in Dark Souls arises from how [late '00s and early 2010s] games have conditioned us. Gamers are used to handholding tutorials that walk you through every aspect of a game’s mechanics." While complimenting the game's notoriously steep difficulty curve, Kollar was less favourable toward its "overall lack of direction".
In a review of Dark Souls in Black Gate, Connor Gormley said "I can't help but smile at all the things I've done in this game, from the serious and atmospheric, to the actually kind of stupid, like losing a fist fight with a giant mushroom man who I like to imagine has a thick cockney accent. I've given very few examples of the game's lore by design, because half of the fun is finding that out for yourself, at least if you're in it for the fantasy. sections.Reception / Original release / Later rel:
